claim: Progenitors of the thoracic tracheal system of adult Drosophila (tracheoblasts) arrest in G2 during larval life.
source: Progenitors of the thoracic tracheal system of adult Drosophila (tracheoblasts) arrest in G2 during larval life and rekindle a mitotic program subsequently.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational observation.

claim: G2 arrest in tracheoblasts is dependent on ATR-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1.
source: G2 arrest is dependent on ataxia telangiectasia mutated and rad3-related kinase (ATR)-dependent phosphorylation of checkpoint kinase 1 (Chk1) that is actuated in the absence of detectable DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited (Kizhedathu et al., 2018; Kizhedathu et al., 2020).

claim: ATR-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 in tracheoblasts is actuated in the absence of detectable DNA damage.
source: G2 arrest is dependent on ataxia telangiectasia mutated and rad3-related kinase (ATR)-dependent phosphorylation of checkpoint kinase 1 (Chk1) that is actuated in the absence of detectable DNA damage.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) are high in arrested tracheoblasts.
source: Here we report that levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) are high in arrested tracheoblasts and decrease upon mitotic re-entry.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by H2DCFDA and DHE staining data shown in Figure 1B-I.

claim: ROS levels decrease upon mitotic re-entry in tracheoblasts.
source: Here we report that levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) are high in arrested tracheoblasts and decrease upon mitotic re-entry.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by H2DCFDA and DHE staining data at 32-40 hr L3 shown in Figure 1E and I.

claim: High ROS in tracheoblasts is dependent on expression of Duox.
source: High ROS is dependent on expression of Duox, an H2O2 generating dual oxidase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ROS reporter data in Duox knockdown animals shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: Duox is an H2O2 generating dual oxidase.
source: High ROS is dependent on expression of Duox, an H2O2 generating dual oxidase.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is established knowledge about Duox function.

claim: ROS quenching by overexpression of superoxide dismutase 1 abolishes Chk1 phosphorylation.
source: ROS quenching by overexpression of superoxide dismutase 1, or by knockdown of Duox, abolishes Chk1 phosphorylation and results in precocious proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pChk1 immunostaining data in btl-SOD1 animals shown in Figure 1N.

claim: ROS quenching by knockdown of Duox abolishes Chk1 phosphorylation.
source: ROS quenching by overexpression of superoxide dismutase 1, or by knockdown of Duox, abolishes Chk1 phosphorylation and results in precocious proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pChk1 immunostaining data in btl-DuoxRNAi animals shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ROS quenching results in precocious proliferation of tracheoblasts.
source: ROS quenching by overexpression of superoxide dismutase 1, or by knockdown of Duox, abolishes Chk1 phosphorylation and results in precocious proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell number and mitotic index data shown in Figures 1L-M and 2G-H.

claim: Tracheae deficient in Duox can induce phosphorylation of Chk1 in response to micromolar concentrations of H2O2 in minutes.
source: Tracheae deficient in Duox, or deficient in both Duox and regulators of DNA damage-dependent ATR/Chk1 activation (ATRIP/TOPBP1/claspin), can induce phosphorylation of Chk1 in response to micromolar concentrations of H2O2 in minutes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pChk1 immunostaining data after H2O2 treatment shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Tracheae deficient in both Duox and ATRIP/TOPBP1/claspin can induce phosphorylation of Chk1 in response to micromolar concentrations of H2O2 in minutes.
source: Tracheae deficient in Duox, or deficient in both Duox and regulators of DNA damage-dependent ATR/Chk1 activation (ATRIP/TOPBP1/claspin), can induce phosphorylation of Chk1 in response to micromolar concentrations of H2O2 in minutes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pChk1 immunostaining data in double knockdown animals after H2O2 treatment shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: H2O2 activates ATR/Chk1 in tracheoblasts by a non-canonical, potentially direct, mechanism.
source: The findings presented reveal that H2O2 activates ATR/Chk1 in tracheoblasts by a non-canonical, potentially direct, mechanism.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the independence from ATRIP/TOPBP1/claspin and absence of DNA damage.

claim: ATR and Chk1 are essential for DNA damage repair and for normal development.
source: Ataxia telangiectasia mutated and rad3-related kinase (ATR, Mei-41) and its substrate, checkpoint kinase 1 (Chk1, Grapes), are essential for DNA damage repair and for normal development (Artus and Cohen-Tannoudji, 2008; Blythe and Wieschaus, 2015; Cimprich and Cortez, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The mechanism by which ATR phosphorylates and activates Chk1 in response to DNA damage has been well characterized.
source: The mechanism by which ATR phosphorylates and activates Chk1 in response to DNA damage and the mechanism by which activated Chk1 induces cell cycle arrest have been well characterized (Choi et al., 2010; Cimprich and Cortez, 2008; Delacroix et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2012; Xu and Leffak, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The mechanisms for the activation of ATR/Chk1 during development are less well understood.
source: In contrast, the mechanisms for the activation of ATR/Chk1 during development, and the roles of these proteins therein, are less well understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction to establish the knowledge gap.

claim: The ATR/Chk1 axis is co-opted during Drosophila development for inducing G2 arrest in progenitor cells.
source: We reported recently that the ATR/Chk1 axis is co-opted during Drosophila development for inducing G2 arrest in progenitor cells (Kizhedathu et al., 2018; Kizhedathu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Progenitors of the adult tracheal system in Drosophila remain mitotically quiescent through larval life.
source: The progenitors of the adult tracheal (respiratory) system in Drosophila remain mitotically quiescent through larval life and rekindle cell divisions at the onset of pupariation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: Tracheoblasts are arrested in the G2 phase of the cell cycle for approximately 56 hours.
source: Progenitors of the tracheal branches of the second thoracic metamere (Tr2, hereafter referred to as tracheoblasts) are arrested in the G2 phase of the cell cycle for ~56 hr and divide thereafter (Djabrayan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: G2 arrest in tracheoblasts is dependent on ATR-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1.
source: Importantly, we have shown previously that G2 arrest in tracheoblasts is dependent on ATR-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction referencing previous work.

claim: Arrested tracheoblasts phosphorylate Chk1 in the absence of detectable DNA damage.
source: First, arrested tracheoblasts phosphorylate Chk1 (phosphorylated Chk1 [pChk1]) in the absence of detectable DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key observation from previous work.

claim: Chk1 is upregulated by a Wnt signaling-dependent mechanism in arrested tracheoblasts.
source: Second, Chk1 is upregulated by a Wnt signaling-dependent mechanism in arrested tracheoblasts and high levels of Chk1 expression are necessary to induce arrest (Kizhedathu et al., 2018; Kizhedathu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: High levels of Chk1 expression are necessary to induce arrest in tracheoblasts.
source: Second, Chk1 is upregulated by a Wnt signaling-dependent mechanism in arrested tracheoblasts and high levels of Chk1 expression are necessary to induce arrest (Kizhedathu et al., 2018; Kizhedathu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ATR and related kinases ATM and DNA-PK are the principal sensors of DNA damage and effectors of the DNA damage response.
source: Although ATR and the related kinases ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and DNA-PK are the principal sensors of DNA damage and effectors of the DNA damage response (Durocher and Jackson, 2001), there is evidence that these kinases can also be activated by non-canonical mechanisms that are not dependent on DNA damage (Guo et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ATR, ATM, and DNA-PK can be activated by non-canonical mechanisms that are not dependent on DNA damage.
source: Although ATR and the related kinases ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and DNA-PK are the principal sensors of DNA damage and effectors of the DNA damage response (Durocher and Jackson, 2001), there is evidence that these kinases can also be activated by non-canonical mechanisms that are not dependent on DNA damage (Guo et al., 2010; Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ROS can directly activate ATM by stabilizing ATM homodimers through the formation of intermolecular disulfide bridges.
source: Pertinently, there is evidence that ROS can directly activate ATM by stabilizing ATM homodimers through the formation of intermolecular disulfide bridges (Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: ROS-activated ATM can phosphorylate and activate substrates like checkpoint kinase 2 (Chk2).
source: ROS-activated ATM can phosphorylate and activate substrates like checkpoint kinase 2 (Chk2).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: ROS can activate ATR and lead to Chk1 phosphorylation via the induction of DNA damage.
source: There is evidence that ROS can activate ATR and lead to Chk1 phosphorylation via the induction of DNA damage (Srinivas et al., 2019; Willis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mechanical stress on the nuclear envelope can lead to ATR activation.
source: A recent study has shown that mechanical stress on the nuclear envelope, arising during DNA replication (S phase) or in response to osmotic stress or mechanical stimulation, can lead to ATR activation (Kumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: ATR can be activated by a non-canonical mechanism.
source: This implies that ATR can also be activated by a non-canonical mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from the mechanical stress study.

claim: ROS are important regulators of developmental processes.
source: ROS are now generally recognized as important regulators of developmental processes (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The Drosophila genome encodes two NADPH oxidases – NOX and dual oxidase (Duox).
source: Interestingly, the Drosophila genome encodes two NADPH oxidases – NOX and dual oxidase (Duox) (Kim and Lee, 2014) – and one of these, Duox, is expressed at high levels in the larval tracheal system (Robinson et al., 2013 ).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Duox is expressed at high levels in the larval tracheal system.
source: Interestingly, the Drosophila genome encodes two NADPH oxidases – NOX and dual oxidase (Duox) (Kim and Lee, 2014) – and one of these, Duox, is expressed at high levels in the larval tracheal system (Robinson et al., 2013 ).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Duox catalyzes the oxidation of NADPH, leading to the generation of H2O2.
source: Duox catalyzes the oxidation of NADPH, leading to the generation of H2O2 (Bedard and Krause, 2007; Geiszt et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Tracheoblasts are in the G1 phase at the time the embryo hatches into a larva.
source: Analysis of the cell cycle phasing of tracheoblasts using the fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator (FUCCI) system (Zielke et al., 2014) has shown that the cells are in the G1 phase at the time the embryo hatches into a larva and that the cells transition from G1 to S to G2 in the first larval instar (L1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Tracheoblasts transition from G1 to S to G2 in the first larval instar (L1).
source: Analysis of the cell cycle phasing of tracheoblasts using the fluorescent ubiquitination-based cell cycle indicator (FUCCI) system (Zielke et al., 2014) has shown that the cells are in the G1 phase at the time the embryo hatches into a larva and that the cells transition from G1 to S to G2 in the first larval instar (L1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Tracheoblasts remain in G2 from the second larval instar (L2) till mid third larval instar (L3) (32–40 hr L3, ~56 hr).
source: Tracheoblasts remain in G2 from the second larval instar (L2) till mid third larval instar (L3) (32–40 hr L3, ~56 hr) and divide rapidly thereafter (Kizhedathu et al., 2018; Kizhedathu et al., 2020, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Levels of H2DCFDA are readily detectable in tracheoblasts at L2.
source: Analysis of H2DCFDA and DHE staining in tracheoblasts at various stages revealed that levels of both reporters are readily detectable at L2 (Figure 1B and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Levels of DHE are readily detectable in tracheoblasts at L2.
source: Analysis of H2DCFDA and DHE staining in tracheoblasts at various stages revealed that levels of both reporters are readily detectable at L2 (Figure 1B and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Levels of H2DCFDA and DHE are nearly undetectable at 32–40 hr L3 in wild type animals.
source: and nearly undetectable at 32–40 hr L3 in wild type (btl-Gal4) animals (Figure 1E, I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E and I.

claim: Cytoplasmic ROS is high in arrested cells and low in mitotically active cells.
source: Taken together, the analysis of ROS reporters (Figure 1) showed that cytoplasmic ROS is high in arrested cells and low in mitotically active cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the Results section based on the ROS reporter data.

claim: SOD1 is a cytoplasmic enzyme that scavenges ROS.
source: SOD1 is a cytoplasmic enzyme that scavenges ROS (Blackney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Levels of H2DCFDA and DHE are significantly lower in btl-SOD1-expressing animals compared to controls.
source: Levels of H2DCFDA and DHE were found to be significantly lower in btl-SOD1-expressing animals compared to controls (Figure 1J and K, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D, compare with Figure 1B and F, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1J and K.

claim: SOD1 overexpression is an effective way to quench ROS in tracheae.
source: This showed that SOD1 overexpression is an effective way to quench ROS in tracheae.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the ROS reporter data in SOD1-overexpressing animals.

claim: SOD1 overexpression results in precocious cell division from 0 to 8 hr L3.
source: Analysis of the cell numbers and frequency of pH3+ figures in Tr2 showed that SOD1 overexpression resulted in precocious cell division from 0 to 8 hr L3 (Figure 1L and M, n ≥ 7 tracheae per timepoint, Figure 1—source data 1; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1L and M.

claim: Precocious cell divisions in btl-SOD1 tracheae are similar to that observed in Chk1 mutants.
source: We noted that the precocious cell divisions in btl-SOD1 tracheae are similar to that observed in Chk1 mutants (btl-GAL4/UAS-Chk1RNAi (btl-Chk1RNAi), Figure 1L, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1L.

claim: Quenching of ROS phenocopies the loss of Chk1 in tracheoblasts.
source: Based on these data, we concluded that quenching of ROS phenocopies the loss of Chk1 in these cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the similarity of phenotypes.

claim: pChk1 levels are high in L2 and early L3 and diminished at 32–40 hr L3.
source: As reported previously, pChk1 levels are high in L2 and early L3 and diminished at 32–40 hr L3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section referencing previous findings.

claim: pChk1 levels are reduced in btl-SOD1-expressing tracheae compared to wild type at L2 and early L3.
source: pChk1 immunostaining in btl-SOD1-expressing tracheae in L2 and early L3 showed that pChk1 levels were reduced in comparison to wild type at these respective stages (Figure 1N, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1N.

claim: High ROS levels are necessary for G2 arrest in tracheoblasts.
source: We inferred that high ROS levels are necessary for G2 arrest and that high ROS contributes in some manner to high levels of pChk1.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the SOD1 overexpression data.

claim: High ROS contributes to high levels of pChk1 in tracheoblasts.
source: We inferred that high ROS levels are necessary for G2 arrest and that high ROS contributes in some manner to high levels of pChk1.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the correlation between ROS and pChk1 levels.

claim: Duox mRNA levels are higher at L2, 0–8 hr L3, and 16–24 hr L3 than at 32–40 hr L3.
source: Our analysis showed that Duox mRNA levels are higher at L2, 0–8 hr L3, and 16–24 hr L3 than at 32–40 hr L3 (Figure 2A, n ≥ 15 tracheal fragments per timepoint per experiment, n = 3 experiments).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The timecourse of Duox mRNA expression correlates with the timecourse of ROS accumulation in the tracheae.
source: We concluded that the timecourse of Duox mRNA expression correlates with the timecourse of ROS accumulation in the tracheae.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the comparison of Duox expression and ROS levels.

claim: The reduction of Duox leads to a dramatic decrease in levels of H2DCFDA and DHE.
source: The reduction in the levels of Duox using two different RNAi lines (BDSC-32903, BDSC-33975, btl-GAL4/+; UAS-DuoxRNAi/+ (btl-DuoxRNAi)) followed by H2DCFDA and DHE staining showed that the reduction of Duox leads to a dramatic decrease in levels of both the reporters (Figure 2B–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F, compare with Figure 1B and E, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B-E.

claim: The high levels of ROS in arrested tracheoblasts are dependent on Duox expression.
source: Based on these data, we inferred that the high levels of ROS in arrested tracheoblasts are dependent on Duox expression.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on the Duox knockdown data.

claim: The knockdown of Duox results in the loss of pChk1.
source: Consistent with the previous findings with SOD1 overexpression, we observed that the knockdown of Duox resulted in the loss of pChk1 (Figure 2F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals rekindle cell divisions sooner than their wild type counterparts.
source: We found that btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals rekindle cell divisions sooner than their wild type counterparts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on cell number and mitotic index data.

claim: Four Wnt ligands – Wg, Wnt5, Wnt6, and Wnt10 – are expressed by the tracheoblasts.
source: Wnt signaling in the trachea is mediated by four Wnt ligands – Wg, Wnt5, Wnt6, and Wnt10 – that are expressed by the tracheoblasts (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All four Wnt ligands are expressed at high levels in arrested cells and downregulated post-mitotic entry.
source: All ligands are expressed at high levels in arrested cells and downregulated post-mitotic entry.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as background information.

claim: The four Wnts act synergistically to upregulate Chk1 expression.
source: We have also shown that the four Wnts act synergistically to upregulate Chk1 expression but are redundant for expression of other Wnt targets like Fz3.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section referencing previous work.

claim: The expression of all Wnt ligands, Fz3 and Chk1, is comparable in wild type, btl-SOD1 and btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals.
source: We found that the expression of all Wnt ligands, Fz3 and Chk1, was comparable in wild type, btl-SOD1 and btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals (Figure 3B and C, red dashed line marks wild type levels, n ≥ 15 tracheal fragments per timepoint per experiment, n = 3 experiments).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Perturbations in ROS levels in the trachea do not impact Wnt signaling nor expression of Wnt targets like Chk1.
source: This showed that perturbations in ROS levels in the trachea do not impact Wnt signaling nor expression of Wnt targets like Chk1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the qPCR data.

claim: ATR transcript levels do not change in btl-SOD1 and btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals compared to control.
source: We also assayed the levels of ATR in btl-SOD1 and btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals by qPCR and found no change in ATR transcript levels compared to control (Figure 3B and C, red dashed line marks wild type levels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: ROS does not regulate the abundance of either Chk1 or ATR transcripts.
source: Together, the qPCR data suggested that ROS did not regulate the abundance of either Chk1 or ATR transcripts.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the qPCR data.

claim: Precocious mitotic re-entry observed in Wnt signaling-deficient tracheoblasts can be rescued by overexpression of Chk1.
source: We have shown previously that precocious mitotic re-entry observed in Wnt signaling-deficient tracheoblasts (btl-TCFRNAi) can be rescued by overexpression of Chk1 (Kizhedathu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Overexpression of Chk1 in btl-DuoxRNAi-expressing animals does not rescue the precocious proliferation phenotype.
source: We counted numbers of tracheoblasts in btl-GAL4/+; UAS-DuoxRNAi/UAS-Chk1 (btl-DuoxRNAi, Chk1) animals at 16–24 hr L3 to find that the numbers were considerably higher than wild type and comparable to the numbers in btl-DuoxRNAi animals (Figure 3D, n ≥ 7 tracheae, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Overexpression of ATR in btl-DuoxRNAi animals does not rescue the precocious proliferation phenotype.
source: Along these lines, we also overexpressed ATR in btl-DuoxRNAi animals and counted the number of Tr2 tracheoblasts at 16–24 hr L3. We found that the numbers were higher than wild type and comparable to the numbers in btl-DuoxRNAi animals (Figure 3D, n ≥ 7 tracheae, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ROS does not regulate ATR/Chk1 gene expression.
source: Taken together, the analyses suggested that ROS does not regulate ATR/Chk1 gene expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the overexpression experiments.

claim: ATR-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 at serine 373 is necessary for its activation.
source: The ATR-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 at serine 373 is thought to be necessary for its activation (Liu et al., 2000; Patil et al., 2013; Bayer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: A phosphomimic variant of Chk1 (Chk1S373D) can rescue the Duox mutant phenotype.
source: We overexpressed Chk1S373D in btl-DuoxRNAi animals and counted cell numbers in Tr2 at 16–24 hr L3. We found that Tr2 cell numbers in these animals were now comparable to wild type (and lower than in btl-DuoxRNAi animals, Figure 3D, n ≥ 7 tracheae, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ROS is required for ATR-dependent phosphorylation and activation of Chk1.
source: The rescue of the Duox mutant phenotype by the phosphomimic variant of Chk1 suggested that ROS is required for ATR-dependent phosphorylation and activation of Chk1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the rescue experiment.

claim: There is no detectable DNA damage in arrested tracheoblasts using the marker γ-H2AX.
source: However, our analysis of DNA damage in tracheoblasts, using the well-characterized marker for double-strand DNA breaks (γ-H2AX), found no detectable DNA damage in arrested cells (Kizhedathu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Robust 8-oxodG staining is detected in trachea at 1 mM H2O2.
source: Robust staining was detected in trachea at 1 mM H2O2(Figure 4A, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 2), but no signal was detected at lower concentrations or in untreated tracheae.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is no 8-oxodG accumulation in G2-arrested tracheoblasts under normal conditions.
source: This showed that although 8-oxodG accumulation is responsive to oxidative stress, there is no 8-oxodG accumulation in G2-arrested tracheoblasts under normal conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the 8-oxodG staining data.

claim: The accumulation of 8-oxodG in Tr2 tracheoblasts is cytoplasmic.
source: The accumulation of 8-oxodG in Tr2 tracheoblasts was cytoplasmic unlike the tracheal cells in other metameres, where 8-oxodG was observed in both cytoplasm and nucleus (Figure 4B, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Foci of RPA70-GFP can be observed in the nuclei of tracheoblasts exposed to 50 Gy γ-irradiation.
source: Foci of GFP could be observed in the nuclei of tracheoblasts exposed to 50 Gy γ-irradiation (Figure 4C, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3) but no foci were detected in untreated tracheae at the same stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No RPA70-GFP foci are detected in untreated tracheae at L2.
source: Foci of GFP could be observed in the nuclei of tracheoblasts exposed to 50 Gy γ-irradiation (Figure 4C, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3) but no foci were detected in untreated tracheae at the same stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Foci of nuclear γ-H2AX staining are observed in tracheoblasts exposed to 50 Gy of γ-irradiation.
source: We observed foci of nuclear γ-H2AX staining in tracheoblasts exposed to 50 Gy of γ-irradiation (Figure 4D, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3) but not in untreated tracheae at the same stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is no detectable DNA damage in arrested tracheoblasts based on 8-oxodG, RPA70-GFP, and γ-H2AX analysis.
source: Taken together, our analysis of 8-oxodG, RPA70-GFP, and γ-H2AX further confirmed that there is no detectable DNA damage in arrested tracheoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on multiple DNA damage markers.

claim: The activation of ATR/Chk1 in response to DNA damage requires ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin.
source: These studies show that the activation of ATR/Chk1 requires three major proteins: ATR interacting protein (ATRIP, mus-304), topoisomerase II binding protein 1 (TOPBP1, mus-101), and claspin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: DNA damage-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 in Tr2 DT cells requires ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin.
source: This shows that DNA damage-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 in Tr2 DT cells requires ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the γ-irradiation experiments with knockdowns.

claim: The loss of ATR leads to the loss of pChk1 in tracheoblasts.
source: pChk1 staining of the tracheae from these animals revealed that the loss of ATR led to the loss of pChk1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, or claspin does not lead to a loss of pChk1 in L2 tracheoblasts.
source: In contrast, the knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, or claspin did not lead to a loss of pChk1 in L2 (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: The knockdown of ATR leads to an increase in cell number at 16–24 hr L3.
source: While the knockdown of ATR led to an increase in cell number at 16–24 hr L3, knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin did not (Figure 4I, n ≥ seven tracheae per timepoint, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin does not lead to an increase in cell number at 16–24 hr L3.
source: While the knockdown of ATR led to an increase in cell number at 16–24 hr L3, knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin did not (Figure 4I, n ≥ seven tracheae per timepoint, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: ATR-dependent activation of Chk1 in G2-arrested tracheoblasts does not require ATRIP, TOPBP1, or claspin.
source: These data indicate that ATR-dependent activation of Chk1 in G2-arrested tracheoblasts cells does not require ATRIP, TOPBP1, or claspin.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the knockdown experiments.

claim: ROS-dependent Chk1 activation in tracheoblasts does not involve the DNA damage response pathway.
source: Collectively, these experiments lend support to the idea that the ROS-dependent Chk1 activation in tracheoblasts does not involve the DNA damage response pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the independence from DNA damage response components.

claim: Robust pChk1 staining is detected in btl-DuoxRNAi tracheae incubated with H2O2.
source: We detected no pChk1 staining in tracheae exposed to buffer alone and robust pChk1 staining in tracheae incubated with H2O2 (Figure 5B–E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Exposure to H2O2 for periods as short as 2 min is sufficient to restore levels of pChk1 in btl-DuoxRNAi tracheae.
source: Interestingly, we noted that exposure to H2O2 for periods as short as 2 min was sufficient to restore levels of pChk1 in btl-DuoxRNAi tracheae (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is no pChk1 accumulation in btl-ATRRNAi tracheae post H2O2 treatment.
source: We also probed pChk1 levels in btl-ATRRNAi (btl-GAL4/UAS-ATRRNAi) tracheae post H2O2 treatment and found that there was no pChk1 accumulation (Figure 5G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: H2O2 treatment is sufficient to induce Chk1 phosphorylation in an ATR-dependent manner.
source: Together, these data show that H2O2 treatment is sufficient to induce Chk1 phosphorylation in an ATR-dependent manner and that H2O2 can induce pChk1 in minutes.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the H2O2 treatment experiments.

claim: H2O2 can induce pChk1 in minutes.
source: Together, these data show that H2O2 treatment is sufficient to induce Chk1 phosphorylation in an ATR-dependent manner and that H2O2 can induce pChk1 in minutes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on the rapid kinetics observed.

claim: pChk1 can be detected 1 hr post γ-irradiation but not earlier.
source: We could detect pChk1 1 hr post irradiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 2) but not earlier (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: The kinetics of Chk1 phosphorylation in response to H2O2 could be significantly faster than in response to γ-radiation.
source: These experiments suggest that the kinetics of Chk1 phosphorylation in response to H2O2 could be significantly faster than in response to γ-radiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the comparison of kinetics.

claim: The knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin does not prevent the activation of Chk1 by H2O2.
source: pChk1 immunostaining showed that the knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin did not prevent the activation of Chk1 (Figure 5G–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, n ≥ 6 tracheae per condition per experiment, n = 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: H2O2-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 is independent of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin.
source: This strongly suggests that the H2O2-dependent phosphorylation of Chk1 is independent of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on the H2O2 treatment experiments with knockdowns.

claim: Duox-generated H2O2 is required for the activation of ATR/Chk1 axis in tracheoblasts.
source: The findings presented here demonstrate that Duox-generated H2O2 is required for the activation of ATR/Chk1 axis in this context (see model in Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as the main finding and shown in the model in Figure 5J.

claim: The formation of an intermolecular disulfide bond between cysteine residues at the C-terminus of ATM is essential for ATM homodimerization and activation.
source: The formation of an intermolecular disulfide bond between cysteine residues located at the C-terminus of ATM was found to be essential for ATM homodimerization and activation (Guo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The structure of human ATR in complex with ATRIP has been determined by cryoEM.
source: The structure of Drosophila ATR is not known, but the structure of human ATR in complex with ATRIP has been determined by cryoEM and the human ATR-ATRIP complex has been shown to dimerize (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The human ATR-ATRIP complex has been shown to dimerize.
source: The structure of Drosophila ATR is not known, but the structure of human ATR in complex with ATRIP has been determined by cryoEM and the human ATR-ATRIP complex has been shown to dimerize (Rao et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: A model for the Drosophila ATR dimer shows that there are no exposed cysteines that are close enough to form intermolecular disulfide bridges.
source: This model shows that there are no exposed cysteines that are close enough to form intermolecular disulfide bridges.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on structural modeling.

claim: H2O2 may regulate ATR in a different way than what has been proposed for ATM.
source: Thus, there is a possibility that H2O2 regulates ATR in a different way than what has been proposed for ATM.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on structural differences.

claim: The possibility that H2O2 can directly activate ATR by other mechanisms seems likely.
source: The possibility that H2O2 can directly activate ATR by other mechanisms seems likely.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation.

claim: ROS can alter kinase activity either by modifying cysteine residues at or near the active site or more broadly, leading to conformational changes.
source: ROS can alter kinase activity either by modifying cysteine residues at or near the active site or more broadly, leading to conformational changes (Corcoran and Cotter, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Loss of either ATR or Chk1 leads to slow rate of cell division post mitotic reentry.
source: We have shown that loss of either ATR or Chk1 leads to slow rate of cell division post mitotic reentry (Kizhedathu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: There is no evidence for any DNA damage post-mitotic re-entry in tracheoblasts.
source: Since there is no evidence for any DNA damage post-mitotic re-entry and the knockdown of ATRIP, TOPBP1, and claspin does not recapitulate the ATR/Chk1 mutant phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, n ≥ 7 tracheae per timepoint), the mechanism for the activation of ATR/Chk1 post-mitotic re-entry is unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the absence of DNA damage markers.

claim: Neither the overexpression of SOD1 nor the knockdown of Duox recapitulates the mitotic defect observed in ATR/Chk1 mutants.
source: Interestingly, neither the overexpression of SOD1 nor the knockdown of Duox recapitulates the mitotic defect observed in ATR/Chk1 mutants (Figures 1J and 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and shown in Figures 1J and 2F.

claim: There are other non-canonical mechanisms of ATR/Chk1 activation that are relevant to the roles of these kinases during development.
source: This suggests that there are other non-canonical-mechanisms of ATR/Chk1 activation that are relevant to the roles of these kinases during development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the phenotypic differences.

claim: The levels of Chk1 mRNA are regulated transcriptionally by the Wnt signaling pathway.
source: We have previously shown that the levels of Chk1 mRNA are regulated transcriptionally by the Wnt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion referencing previous work.

claim: ROS levels are unaffected in Wnt pathway mutants.
source: We determined whether Wnt signaling also regulates Duox expression and ROS levels. This analysis showed that ROS levels are unaffected in Wnt pathway mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on unpublished data.

claim: Wnt signaling pathway does not regulate Duox nor ROS levels.
source: We infer that Wnt signaling pathway does not regulate Duox nor ROS levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an inference from the Wnt mutant analysis.

claim: Juvenile hormone (JH) has been shown to act as a negative regulator of cell proliferation in tracheae.
source: Juvenile hormone (JH) has been shown to act as a negative regulator of cell proliferation in tracheae (Djabrayan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The levels of JH are high in L2 and early L3 and drop mid L3.
source: Pertinently, the levels of JH are high in L2 and early L3 and drop mid L3 (Dubrovsky, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The timecourse of JH levels parallels the timecourses of both Duox and Chk1 expression.
source: Thus, the timecourse of JH levels parallels the timecourses of both Duox and Chk1 expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an observation.

claim: Ovarian cancer cells that express high levels of Duox1 and high levels of activated Chk1 are relatively Cisplatin-resistant.
source: It has been reported that ovarian cancer cells that express high levels of Duox1 and high levels of activated Chk1 are relatively Cisplatin-resistant (Meng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: High levels of Chk1 activation are critical for chemoresistance in ovarian cancer cells.
source: The authors suggest that high levels of Chk1 activation are critical for chemoresistance and that the high levels of Chk1 activation are likely the result of ROS-generated DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion referencing another study's interpretation.

claim: High ROS may independently activate Chk1 and contribute toward chemoresistance.
source: The findings presented here suggest that high ROS may independently activate Chk1 and contribute toward chemoresistance.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on the current findings.

claim: Cancer cells that have high levels of ROS and an active DNA damage repair pathway have been shown to be relatively radioresistant.
source: Along the same lines, cancer cells that have high levels of ROS (Gu et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2020) and an active DNA damage repair pathway have been shown to be relatively radioresistant (Alsubhi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: ROS-based activation of ATR/Chk1 may contribute toward the observed chemo-/radioresistance of cancer cells.
source: We suggest that the ROS-based activation of ATR/Chk1 activation evidenced here may also contribute toward the observed chemo-/radioresistance of cancer cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a speculation based on the current findings.
